headline: Man saved from rubble after eight days

sources.title: Man pulled from rubble in 'miraculous' rescue 8 days after Venezuela earthquakes - CNN
'Miracle': Trapped man rescued eight days after Venezuela earthquakes - Al Jazeera
Venezuelan security guard pulled alive from earthquake rubble after 8 days - PBS News
Venezuelan security guard rescued 8 days after twin earthquakes (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: Eight days after two [[powerful]] earthquakes hit Venezuela, [[rescuers]] have {{pulled a man out}} of a [[collapsed]] building, and he is still alive. The man, a security guard named Hernan Gil, was [[trapped]] when a shopping mall parking lot {{came down}} [[on top of]] him in the coastal town of La Guaira. Doctors say he is now [[in good condition]]. Many people are calling the rescue a [[miracle]].

verbs.wrong: To help someone walk out of a dangerous place
verbs.correct: To remove someone from a dangerous place
verbs.why: Divers pull a swimmer out of rough water, and firefighters pull people out of a burning building. Rescuers pulled Hernan Gil out of the collapsed parking lot in La Guaira after eight days trapped underground.

A tree branch can come down in a strong wind, and an old building can come down in seconds during an earthquake. The shopping mall parking lot came down on top of Gil in La Guaira when the ground shook.

chunks.text: When the building fell, Gil {{ended up}} trapped inside a small concrete booth in the basement. Experts say the strong booth {{held up}} and formed a protective pocket that shielded him from the falling [[debris]]. For eight long days, he {{held on}} under [[tons of]] [[rubble]], with no food and very little water.

verbs.wrong: To hide somewhere to stay safe
verbs.correct: To finally be in a particular situation
verbs.why: You can take a wrong turn and end up in a town you never planned to visit. Gil ended up trapped inside a small concrete booth in the basement when the parking lot collapsed above him.

verbs.wrong: To be rebuilt after the earthquake ended
verbs.correct: To stay strong and not fall or fail
verbs.why: An old ladder can still hold up even when it looks shaky, though not every wall holds up during a real earthquake. In La Guaira, the small concrete booth held up and protected Gil from the falling debris above.

verbs.wrong: To stay calm and quiet in danger
verbs.correct: To survive or continue in a hard situation
verbs.why: A rider holds on tightly as a roller coaster drops, and a lost hiker might hold on until help finally arrives. Gil held on for eight days underground with almost no food and very little water.

chunks.text: Rescue teams from seven countries {{teamed up}} to save him. According to Chile's fire department, it took more than 70 hours of [[careful]] work to {{dig out}} the security booth. The workers [[refused]] to {{give up}}, [[even though]] [[the best chance]] of finding [[survivors]] usually ends after about three days. [[In the end]], their effort {{paid off}}.

verbs.wrong: To arrive at the same time
verbs.correct: To join together to work with others
verbs.why: Small businesses can team up for a big sale, and two towns often team up after a storm to share equipment. Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up in Venezuela to save the trapped security guard.

verbs.wrong: To break a hole in something hard
verbs.correct: To remove someone or something by digging
verbs.why: Workers dig a car out of deep snow after a blizzard, and rescuers sometimes dig out a trapped dog from under rubble. It took Chile's fire department and other crews more than 70 hours to dig out the booth where Gil was trapped.

A person might almost give up on a hard puzzle after an hour, but a good coach tells you never to give up on a goal. The rescue workers in La Guaira refused to give up even after the usual survival window had passed.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result after effort
verbs.why: Years of saving can pay off the day you finally buy a house, and months of hard training pay off on race day. The rescuers' more than 70 hours of careful digging finally paid off when they found Gil alive.

chunks.text: At the hospital, doctors say Gil is slowly {{getting over}} his [[terrible]] [[ordeal]]. The [[twin]] earthquakes have {{turned out}} to be [[among the worst]] in Venezuela's history, killing more than 2,500 people. Thousands of families still do not know what happened to their [[missing]] relatives. For a country [[full of]] sadness, this one rescue has {{brought about}} a [[rare]] moment of hope.

verbs.wrong: To share his story with local reporters
verbs.why: It can take weeks to get over a bad cold, and some people never fully get over a hard loss. At the hospital, doctors say Gil is slowly getting over the experience, though it will take time.

verbs.wrong: To be reported in the news many times
verbs.correct: To finally become a certain way
verbs.why: A job interview can turn out much easier than you feared, and a rainy morning sometimes turns out sunny by noon. The twin earthquakes that trapped Gil turned out to be among the deadliest in Venezuela's history.

verbs.wrong: To remind people of something good
verbs.why: A new coach can bring about a change in a team's attitude, and a new law can bring about big changes for a town. In a country full of sadness after the earthquakes, this one rescue has brought about a rare moment of hope.

mainIdea.s: Rescuers pulled a security guard out of a collapsed parking lot alive after eight days. A strong concrete booth had protected him, and teams from seven countries dug for 70 hours.
mainIdea.why: The booth held up and made a safe pocket around him. Rescuers from seven countries needed more than 70 hours of careful work to reach it.

mainIdea.s: Eight days after the earthquakes, workers reached a security guard who was still alive. He had food and water passed down to him, and doctors say he will need months to recover.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he had no food and very little water for those eight days. Doctors say he is in good condition and is already getting over the ordeal.

mainIdea.s: Two powerful earthquakes have killed more than 2,500 people in Venezuela, and the government is asking other countries for help. Thousands of damaged homes must now be rebuilt.
mainIdea.why: The earthquakes are only the background here. This story is about one man being pulled out alive after eight days.

tf.s: For eight long days, the concrete booth held on and formed a protective pocket around him
tf.why: A structure cannot actively endure the way a person does, so calling it held on instead of held up is unambiguous.

tf.s: In the end, the rescuers' effort paid off and they saved the man alive.
tf.why: The workers refused to give up, and in the end their effort paid off (brought a good result).

tf.s: After more than 70 hours of digging, the rescue teams gave up before finding the man
tf.why: The rescue workers refused to give up. Their effort paid off after more than 70 hours and they found the man alive.

tf.s: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up to save the trapped man.
tf.why: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up (joined together) to save him.

tf.s: Doctors say Gil is slowly getting over his terrible ordeal.
tf.why: At the hospital, doctors say he is slowly getting over (recovering from) the ordeal and is now in good condition.

tf.s: Gil brought about his own terrible ordeal under the rubble.
tf.why: Gil did not cause what happened to him. Bring about means to cause something to happen, but it was the earthquake that trapped him. Doctors say he is getting over the ordeal.

lines.text: Did you hear about the man in Venezuela? The one they {{pulled out}} of a collapsed building?
The security guard? Eight days under the rubble, right?
Eight days. The whole parking lot {{came down}} on him, but he {{ended up}} inside a small concrete booth. [[Somehow]] it {{held up}} and protected him.
No food, almost no water. [[I can't imagine]] how he {{held on}} that long.
[[Me neither]]. Rescue teams from seven countries {{teamed up}} to find him. It took them 70 hours just to {{dig out}} the booth.
[[Wow]]. Most rescues stop after three days, don't they?
Usually, yes. But they refused to {{give up}}, and it {{paid off}}.
In good condition, they say. He'll need time to {{get over}} it, but he's alive.
After everything that's happened there, that country needed some good news.
[[That's what everyone's saying]]. One rescue {{brought about}} a little bit of hope.
